slide_018.text: On this slide, the focus is DEMAND & REQUIREMENTS OF TEMPERATURE DURING PRE-TREATMENT, APPLICATION & CURING OF COATINGS. The important point is to understand exactly what the slide requires and how that requirement affects inspection and coating work. The slide identifies the following key points. During pre-treatment: The surface should normally be at least 3°C above the dew point. The surface must be free from visible moisture, frost, ice and condensation. Coat the prepared surface before rusting or contamination occurs. During application: Apply paint only within the specified temperature range. Low temperature causes: High viscosity and slow drying & curing During curing: Low temperature causes the coating soft, tacky or under-cured. High temperature leads to bubbling, solvent entrapment or rapid surface curing. Consider temperature when checking minimum and maximum over-coating intervals. Note: The coating manufacturer’s technical data sheet, application guide and project specification take priority over general temperature limits. For inspection purposes, pay particular attention to this stated point: During pre-treatment: The surface should normally be at least 3°C above the dew point.. slide_036.text: On this slide, the focus is DEHUMIDIFICATION. The important point is to understand exactly what the slide requires and how that requirement affects inspection and coating work. The slide identifies the following key points. Dehumidification Process: Air Intake: A fan draws warm, humid air from a room into the unit. Cooling: The air passes over a cold evaporator coil, typically part of a refrigeration system. Condensation: Because the coil is colder than the air's dew point (the temperature at which vapor turns to liquid), water vapor in the air changes into liquid droplets on the cold coil. Drainage: This condensed water collects and drips into a collection pan, then flows out through a drain hose, effectively removing moisture from the air. Reheating (Optional but Common): The now-cooled, dehumidified air then passes over the warm condenser coil (the "hot" side of the refrigeration cycle) to be reheated slightly before being blown back into the room, making the space more comfortable without feeling clammy.
